ops.html: Two more findings fill in the picture. Using Premier League player-cam footage, Jordet's team compared 118 Premier League players with Dutch amateur players: the professionals scanned significantly more, and Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard were the top two (Sky Sports, 2021). An eye-tracking study of four elite midfielders in real 11 v 11 matches found that their eyes settled on one spot in only 2.3% of scans, and that they saw more opponents than teammates when they looked (Aksum et al., 2021). In other words, a good scan is a quick snapshot, not a long stare.

ops.anchor: Two situations where one look decides it
ops.html:
How does scanning change by position?

Every position scans, but the moment and the target change. Central midfielders need a picture all the way round because pressure can come from any side. Defenders scan for runners behind them. Wingers and strikers scan for the defender on their back and the space behind the line. In the Premier League study, central midfielders and center backs scanned the most.

PositionWhen to lookWhat to look for
GoalkeeperBefore a back pass reaches youThe striker pressing you, which full-back is free, how much time you have
Center backBefore the keeper passes to you, and as a cross comes inThe free full-back or midfielder; runners behind you at the back post
Full-backBefore you receive near the touchlineHow close their winger is, whether the line ahead is open, the pass inside
Central midfielderBefore every pass to you, both shouldersWho is on your back, which side to turn, the free player on the far side
Number 10Before you receive between their linesA center back stepping out behind you, the gap he leaves, your runners
WingerBefore you receive, while their full-back sets upHow tight he is, who covers behind him, who is arriving in the box
StrikerBefore a pass into your feet, and before a crossThe center back on your back, the gap between the center backs, the keeper's position

The same study found scanning dropped near the touchlines. Near the line, pressure can only come from a few directions. In the middle of the pitch you can be closed from anywhere, so the look matters even more there. Our position packs for the winger, number 10, striker and defender have 20 situations each built around these pictures.

ops.anchor: How can you practise scanning while watching matches?
ops.html:
How do you remember to scan in a match?

Tie the look to something that happens every few seconds in a game, so you don't have to remember it. The best trigger is a teammate getting the ball: as soon as he takes his first touch, check your shoulder, before he looks up to pass to you. Drills build the movement; triggers carry it into matches.

  • Teammate's touch = your look. His first touch is your signal to check the side you can't see.
  • Ball in the air = two looks. A goal kick or long pass gives you time, so check both shoulders.
  • Say one word in your head. "Man on", "turn" or "free". A word turns the look into a decision.
  • Set a 10-minute target. Look before every pass you receive in the first 10 minutes. At half-time, be honest about how often you did.
  • Find the surprise. After the match, note one moment a defender surprised you. That is the moment you didn't look.

Between sessions, our free football scanning test trains the other half of the skill: how much you keep from one 2-second look, with a score out of 10.

faq_add.q: At what age should you start scanning in soccer?
faq_add.a: At any age. Young players can start with simple head-up games while dribbling. From about 15, add looks timed to the pass and drills where the look decides your first touch, like turning away from a friend who changes sides.

faq_add.q: Is scanning the same as peripheral vision?
faq_add.a: No. Peripheral vision is what you notice at the edge of your sight while you watch the ball. Scanning means turning your head to see what your eyes can't reach, mostly behind you. You need both, but only a scan shows you the player on your back.

faq_add.q: How do I remember to scan during a game?
faq_add.a: Link the look to a trigger. Each time a teammate takes a touch, check your shoulder before he looks up to pass. Set a target for the first 10 minutes, then ask yourself honestly at half-time how often you really looked.

faq_add.q: Can you test how well you scan?
faq_add.a: Yes. Unscouted's free football scanning test shows a match picture for 2 seconds, hides the players and asks where the free teammate or the pressure was. On the pitch, count your shoulder checks on video or call a friend's fingers behind you.
